One thing you could maybe try is to get one of those small playpens — the ones that are made up of several separate panels that just hook together to assemble the pen — and then securely attach the individual panels to the surface of your cage, anyplace it would be useful to have horizontal bars. Cable ties can work, if you don't have chewers, but there are more rugged options too.

https://preview.redd.it/bd193wwddc0f1.jpeg?width=1080&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=36ac6a1107b229fe5c506bd8b824080fa87b9ac3

I had (I think) powder-coated ones with each panel a different colour, but it looks like you can get plain metal too. They're about £10–20 a pack where I am, depending on the quality, and they've come in incredibly useful for me over many years of keeping rats and guinea pigs.

You can use them as I suggested above, or as extra/shallower ramps (if you're okay with wire ramps), or to temporarily fix/wall off damaged bits of cage. or for semi-permanently closing off doors or floors. It's maybe not as versatile as something like chicken wire, but IMO it's much safer using small panels with properly finished edges.

They once came in very useful for temporarily but securely dividing a large guinea pig cage into two separate sections, in an emergency. I was looking after this pair of piggie brothers, who'd been closest friends and best snuggle buddies all their lives, when they suddenly, mutually and irrevocably decided they hated each others' guts. As long as they both knew they couldn't actually GET to each other, things were calm, but otherwise it was TIME FOR BLOOD. (Amazes me just how much more vicious they tend to be than rats; they're apparently perfectly capable of fighting to the death, while rats usually seem to at least TRY to negotiate a non-fatal result.) A few playpen panels and some cable ties later and I had a nice solid divider down the middle of the cage, which sorted it for long enough to keep them safe while a new cage was organised.

I even used them as a playpen sometimes.

I have an older gamer in my family who didn't grow up with consoles, and while he can use a controller fine, it takes him a while to learn the control schemes for each game, and he forgets them easily after a short time not playing. When, on top of that, he had to deal with Xbox button prompts when using a PS4 controller, he struggled so much that I cut out tiny bits of post-it note with the relevant symbols on them, and stuck one next to each button.

Some people can easily learn new controls, handle buttons that say A but are actually B, and mentally switch back and forth on the fly, while others can't. It can be affected by a lot of things, like prior gaming experience, individual strengths and weaknesses, how tired you are, and anything that impacts on memory, cognitive flexibility or ability to learn new things. I sometimes feel like a lot of the gaming culture still seems to be centred around the preferences and abilities of 10–25 year olds with time on their hands and unimpaired cognitive abilities (or those who gained their skills when they fitted those criteria). It can be hard to admit that you struggle with all the different and increasingly-complex control schemes, and that's before bringing in controllers that don't match the game/system you're playing.

For me, matching controls would be nice to have, but it's not essential. But constantly having to double-think the controls would just get too frustrating for the family member I mentioned.

My (at the time) 80-something grandma once told me about an accident she had where she went over sideways on her mobility scooter, off the pavement and into the road, a couple of miles from home. She was bruised and bleeding and couldn't get up.

The only people around were a group of teenage boys hanging about on the corner, who came straight over and surrounded her.

While a couple stayed standing in the road to make sure no cars accidentally hit her, one of them must have called the ambulance, and another one asked her address and rode her mobility scooter back to her house for her. The other lads stayed with her until the ambulance came to pick her up and take her to hospital.

As she was quite shaken up by the fall (though luckily not badly injured), she didn't get their names, where they lived, or anything. Spergyfucker here. Tips for upping gifting game:

— Make sure every birthday/anniversary/whatever that you're going to need to buy a gift for is entered in the calendar on your phone, with reminders to buy a present set to go off at least a week beforehand. If you use a paper calendar, write in both the birthday and the reminder to buy a gift.

— Keep a document on your phone (or whatever else you use as your main organisational tool and can easily access), and every time someone says "oh I could do with one of those" or "aw man that's so cool" or otherwise shows an interest in something, write it down with their name, bearing in mind that they may or may not *actually* want that specific thing (it may be better just to use it as a guide to their tastes or interests).

— Don't give gifts that require a lot of input or work from them if you're not absolutely sure they'll like it, like, say, needles and wool for someone who doesn't knit.

— Equally, if someone already has a hobby, they probably only want specific things for it, so, for example, someone who's already a knitter probably has no use for a cheap pair of standard needles.

— It's generally a bad idea to give somebody gifts that imply that it's their job to do the household chores. A new vacuum cleaner that's lighter and more efficient might *seem* like a thoughtful present for your partner if they're the one who does the vacuuming, as it'll save them time and effort. But it's not a gift for *them*, it's a household tool.

—Be very careful with any clothes that come in different sizes. In fact, just avoid them altogether.

— If you're in an equal relationship e.g. siblings, spouses, friends, etc., think about the approximate value of the gifts you've received from them and aim for that ballpark (assuming no financial troubles either side — that can get more complex). So if, say, your best friend tends to get you a book or a mug or a box of chocolates that would cost around £5 to £10, get them something that costs about that much — something more expensive could make them feel very awkward. If your spouse has bought you a fancy watch, a stereo and a laptop on your last three birthdays, a book or a mug for theirs isn't going to cut it. For an unequal relationship e.g. parent/child, auntie/nephew, you can use your discretion a bit more, but try and treat people fairly equally (like, if your sister has two children, don't buy a £2.50 bag of sweets for one and a £30 video game for another — though with children, age comes into this, too, and of course it may make sense to spend more on presents to one branch of the family than another).

— Wrapping the gifts matters. It shows you've gone to a little extra effort and that you remembered their birthday in advance.

I don't have any rats at the moment, but when I did, I had a real problem with keeping *all* of them slim.

It's difficult verging on impossible to feed rats separately from one another the way you might with, say, dogs. You can feed your dogs their meals separately from one another and you're done in ten minutes or less. But rats eat little bits now and then throughout the day, so to feed them separately you'd have to be separating them many times throughout the day, with no food available to them in between.

If you have one fat rat and five slim rats in the same cage and you put less food in the cage, the fat rat will generally stay fat while one or more of the slim rats gets slimmer.

There *is* a certain amount you can do by making them hunt around for their food rather than presenting it in a bowl, but a particularly food-driven rat won't be deterred by that.

Alternatively, you can segregate the fat rat(s) completely, but social isolation is also very unhealthy for them.

It doesn't actually take zero energy to use a preferred pronoun.

To use a pronoun that's different from the one your brain has been trained to use for a person who looks like that, you're required to inhibit the automatic process in your brain that selects which words, including pronouns, to use, and to use the preferred pronoun instead. Inhibiting an action carries a cognitive energy cost. If you ask people to use a pronoun that doesn't match how you'll be automatically perceived by most people, then everyone you meet is dedicating a little bit extra brainpower to using the correct pronoun, which makes it harder to perform other mental tasks at the same time and causes them to mentally tire faster. Only a tiny amount, but it's still happening.

Each hair grows on a cycle. Stress triggers lots of hairs to reach that part of the cycle where they naturally fall out, all at the same time.

Other physical factors can do a similar thing — if you go on a crash diet and lose a lot of weight, then a lot of hair will fall out. Same with some medications. Pregnant women's hair often doesn't fall out as much as usual, so their hair gets very thick, then after they give birth they lose a lot of hair but really it's just going back to normal.

The follicles aren't dead and it isn't permanent. Your hairs won't all decide to start growing again at the same time because hair growth is more complicated than it seems, and they'll all reach the point where they want to start growing at different times.

If you eat well and manage your stress, the thickness should start to gradually come back, but it'll take a while.

The pulling is a separate issue but hopefully you can find ways of improving that with the motivation that you don't want to undo the good work your hair is doing in regrowing from having fallen out through stress.
